PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hospital — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a hospital is and who works inside, so the big building feels like the helper it is.

What is this?

A hospital is a big place where doctors and nurses help people get better — broken arms, fevers, check-ups, and brand-new babies.

What does it mean?

Everyone helping everyone is the idea: a hospital is the town’s biggest promise that nobody is left hurt.

What does the child need to know?

You need to know your name and your grown-up’s name — hospitals ask both kindly. Wristbands go on, stickers come off (onto you).

Why this matters

Some hurts are too big for home — the hospital keeps everything a body could need in one building, with people who practice helping every single day.

What it teaches

Naming body feelings (hurts, hot, dizzy), trusting helpers, sitting through a wait, and the brave skill of letting a stranger with a kind voice look in your ears.

Words to learn

hospitaldoctornursepatientbandagestethoscopewristbandbetter

Say this to your child

“"This is the hospital, where the helpers work. The doctor looks in my ears — bloop! — listens to my heart — thump, thump — and says, all better soon! Sticker, please!"”

Step by step

  1. Walk in together — hands held, name known.
  2. Tell the desk who you are: "I am here with my grown-up."
  3. Wait your turn — hospitals run on turns; the toys are there for the waiting.
  4. Let the doctor look: ears, throat, tummy — say ahh and let the cold disc do its job.
  5. Collect the sticker (non-negotiable), wave goodbye to the nurses, and go home feeling proud.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a big cross sits on the hospital front above rows of windows — almost the whole world agrees that this sign means "people who help are inside".

Ask your child

"Who helps people at the hospital?" (doctors and nurses) "What does the cross on the building mean?" (helpers inside) "What do we tell the desk?" (our name and our grown-up’s name)

What your child can say or do

Your child might bandage every teddy limb in the house, listen to everyone’s heart with a cardboard tube and a very serious face, or hand out stickers after each "check-up" like a tiny discharge nurse.

Out in the real world

Many hospitals run teddy-bear clinics where the toy gets the tour, and knowing the rooms before a real visit changes everything — a familiar hospital is half as scary as a first one. New babies are born here too: hospitals are where towns grow.

Try it together

Hospital for toys: one teddy with a sore paw, one dolly with a cough. Bandage with toilet paper, listen with the tube, write a prescription (a drawing), and finish with a sticker — hospitals always have stickers.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who works at the hospital?" (doctors and nurses) "And what do they do all day?" (help people get better)

This lesson pairs with the Hospital flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.
